01.r: Sets the scene: whenever harvest comes.
01.n: Most of the older translations read 'when'. The BSB's 'If' makes it a case law. The Hebrew particle can carry either sense.

02.r: You cut your grain at harvest.
02.n: Gesenius gives the first sense as TO CUT OFF, especially grain, and so to reap. The KJV and Geneva keep that picture with 'cuttest down'.

03.r: Your crop, the thing being reaped.
03.n: The noun comes from the same root as the verb before it, so the Hebrew reads 'reap your reaping'. The Douay-Rheims says 'the corn', which in older English meant grain. The BSB folds the noun into its verb and does not render it separately.

04.n: Gesenius gives the primary sense as a plain or level tract of country.

05.r: A sheaf left behind by oversight, not on purpose.
05.n: Gesenius cites this very verse for a special sense: to leave something behind through forgetfulness. The Douay-Rheims spells out both halves: 'hast forgot and left'.

06.r: One bound bundle of stalks, left lying in the field.
06.n: BDB separates two words spelled this way: this one, a sheaf, and another, the omer, a dry measure. No Gesenius entry was matched to this word in our parsed copy.

07.r: Still lying where it was cut.

09.r: Do not go back over the field for it.
09.n: This is the ordinary Hebrew verb for turning and returning. Gesenius notes that it is also used figuratively, of a sinner turning back, but here it is literal.

10.n: This is a very common verb, with a meaning as wide as English 'take'. Geneva's 'fet' is an old form of fetch.

11.r: Someone living in Israel who was not born into it.
11.n: Gesenius: a person living out of his own country. STEPBible's lexicon: a newcomer lacking inherited rights. Inherited rights in Israel meant land, so the gēr would usually have no field of their own to reap. That last step is a reasonable reading, not something the lexicons state.

12.r: A child without a father to provide for them.
12.n: Gesenius notes the word is used of a child who has lost only its father. So 'fatherless', which every translation here uses, is more exact than 'orphan'.

13.r: A woman without a husband to provide for her.

14.r: The sheaf now belongs to these three.
14.n: The Hebrew says simply 'it shall be', and the 'to the' on each of the three nouns makes it ownership: it is theirs. The Douay-Rheims follows the Latin Vulgate here and rewords the clause entirely.
t: thou shalt suffer ... to take it away

15.r: Gives the purpose of the law.

16.r: God's blessing is tied to the sheaf left behind.
16.n: Gesenius puts 'to bend the knees, to kneel' first among this verb's senses, ahead of 'to bless'.

17.r: The personal name of Israel's God.
17.n: The translations show four traditions for the name. The KJV, Geneva and Douay-Rheims say 'the Lord', the BSB uses small capitals (LORD), the ASV and YLT say 'Jehovah', and the JPS writes 'HaShem' ('the Name').

18.n: The form is plural but the meaning is singular. In our parsed copy, Gesenius here is only a cross-reference to another entry.

19.r: No part of your work is left out of the blessing.

21.r: The hands that cut the sheaf.
21.n: The form is dual, 'your two hands'. Hebrew uses the dual for things that come in pairs.

_extra.1: δὲ (and, but): added by the Greek translators; nothing in the Hebrew answers to it.

03.n: The Greek has no 'your' here: just 'you reap a harvest'.

07.n: The Greek adds 'your': 'in your field' again, where the Hebrew says 'in the field'.

09.n: Swete's text reads ἀναστραφήσῃ, from ἀναστρέφω, to turn back. Rahlfs's edition reads a longer compound here, ἐπαναστραφήσῃ, so the matched dictionary form (ἐπαναστρέφω) belongs to that reading, not to Swete's.

11.n: The Greek word is προσήλυτος, 'one who has come over'. English 'proselyte' comes from it, though here it still means a resident foreigner, not a religious convert.

17.n: The Greek translators wrote κύριος, 'Lord', for the divine name. It is the same word the servant uses for his master in Matthew 25:24 on this page.
